subject: Pathology
summary: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal‑recessive disorder of branched‑chain amino‑acid catabolism causing toxic accumulation of leucine, isoleucine and valine. Early recognition and metabolic control prevent irreversible neurologic injury.

sections.p: MSUD results from deficiency of the branched‑chain α‑ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex, leading to elevated plasma and urine branched‑chain amino acids (BCAAs). Diagnosis relies on newborn screening or targeted metabolic testing.
b: Plasma leucine > 1000 µmol/L (diagnostic threshold)
Urine organic acid analysis shows elevated branched‑chain ketoacids
Positive tandem mass spectrometry for BCAAs on dried blood spot

t.b: Is there accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine? High levels confirm metabolic block.
Are branched‑chain keto‑acids present? Their presence supports MSUD.
Does the patient have pathogenic variants? Confirms diagnosis and guides counseling.

sections.p: Clinical severity is graded by the classic, intermediate, and thiamine‑responsive forms, reflecting residual BCKDH activity and response to thiamine.
b: Classic: presents in first days of life, severe neurologic crisis
Intermediate: later onset, milder neurologic signs
Thiamine‑responsive: improves with high‑dose thiamine

sections.p: MSUD is genetic; however, secondary metabolic stress (infection, fasting, high‑protein intake) can precipitate crises.
b: Autosomal‑recessive mutations in BCKDHA, BCKDHB, or DBT genes
Catabolic stress (viral infection, malaria, TB) increasing protein breakdown
Inadequate dietary restriction in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Infants develop poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, and a characteristic sweet‑like odor to urine and skin. Neurologic regression, seizures, and hypotonia follow if untreated.
b: Sweet maple‑syrup odor of urine
Rapid neurologic decline after a feeding challenge
Possible cardiomyopathy in severe cases

sections.p: Targeted metabolic testing confirms the diagnosis; imaging evaluates complications.
b: MRI may show diffuse cerebral edema during crisis
Electrolytes to monitor for metabolic acidosis

t.b: Is hyperammonemia present? Elevated ammonia worsens encephalopathy and needs urgent treatment.
Is there metabolic acidosis? Guides bicarbonate therapy.

sections.p: Uncontrolled BCAA accumulation leads to cerebral edema, seizures, coma, and can be fatal within days.
b: Sudden worsening of consciousness
Persistent vomiting despite rehydration
New onset seizures

sections.p: Acute crises require rapid reduction of plasma BCAAs, while long‑term care focuses on dietary restriction and metabolic monitoring.
b: Immediate protein‑free IV fluids with dextrose to halt catabolism
Hemodialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy to clear BCAAs when severe
Lifelong low‑BCAA diet supplemented with a medical formula
Thiamine supplementation in thiamine‑responsive variants

sections.p: Regular monitoring of plasma BCAA levels, growth parameters, and neurodevelopment is essential. Genetic counseling for families is recommended.
b: Quarterly plasma leucine checks in infancy, then semi‑annual
Developmental assessments each clinic visit
Family carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis when available

sections.p: Other inborn errors that cause sweet‑smelling urine or neurologic decline.
b: Phenylketonuria (musty odor, milder neurologic signs)
Isovaleric acidemia (sweaty‑shoe odor)
Organic acidemias with similar metabolic acidosis

sections.p: Early screening may miss mild or thiamine‑responsive forms; normal urine odor does not exclude disease.
b: Normal leucine levels after a prolonged fast can be falsely reassuring
Urine organic acids may be normal during a quiescent phase

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden change in mental status, seizures, or coma in an infant with known or suspected MSUD
Persistent vomiting and inability to feed
Rapidly worsening sweet odor of urine indicating a metabolic crisis

faq.q: Why does urine smell like maple syrup?
faq.a: Excess branched‑chain keto‑acids are excreted, giving a sweet, syrupy odor.
It cannot be cured, but strict dietary control and early treatment prevent severe outcomes.
Only in the thiamine‑responsive subtype; a trial is safe and may reduce BCAA levels.

exam: Describe the biochemical defect in MSUD and its clinical consequences.
Explain how you would manage an acute metabolic crisis in a newborn with MSUD.
List the key investigations needed to confirm the diagnosis and monitor therapy.
